reference.source: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice / Low's Clinical Autonomic Disorders
clinicalPearls: Episodic 'sympathetic storms' after severe acquired brain injury, most often traumatic but also hypoxic-ischaemic or following stroke and haemorrhage
Paroxysms of tachycardia, hypertension, tachypnoea, hyperthermia, sweating, and abnormal extensor posturing
Episodes are often triggered by otherwise innocuous stimuli such as tracheal suctioning, turning, or pain, reflecting an allodynia-like sensitivity
A diagnosis of exclusion: sepsis, seizures, pulmonary embolism, raised intracranial pressure, and drug withdrawal must be ruled out
Typically emerges during recovery from coma, sometimes weeks into the illness, and is associated with more severe injury and longer hospital stay
Diagnostic likelihood tools such as the PSH-Assessment Measure combine clinical features with their severity
Sustained hyperthermia and hypertension risk secondary brain injury and metabolic stress
Management: minimise and avoid triggering stimuli, provide supportive cooling and hydration, and control sympathetic overactivity pharmacologically alongside treating the underlying injury
reference.pathophysiology: Paroxysmal sympathetic hyperactivity follows severe brain injury and reflects a loss of the normal inhibitory control that higher centres exert over spinal and brainstem sympathetic circuits. One influential model proposes that injury disconnects descending inhibitory pathways, leaving excitatory spinal circuits disinhibited, so that ordinarily non-noxious stimuli provoke exaggerated, paroxysmal sympathetic discharges (an 'excitatory-to-inhibitory ratio' disturbance). The result is episodic surges of sympathetic outflow producing tachycardia, hypertension, hyperthermia, sweating, and motor posturing, often with allodynia-like sensitivity to stimulation. The paroxysms subside as recovery progresses, but sustained autonomic and metabolic stress can aggravate secondary brain injury.
additionalDifferentials: Seizure activity, including non-convulsive status epilepticus
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome, serotonin syndrome, or malignant hyperthermia
Pulmonary embolism or another cause of tachycardia and hypoxia
additionalInvestigations: Continuous monitoring of heart rate, blood pressure, temperature, and respiratory rate to document paroxysms
Septic screen with cultures, inflammatory markers, and imaging to exclude infection
EEG to exclude seizures and non-convulsive status epilepticus
Neuroimaging to exclude raised intracranial pressure, hydrocephalus, or rebleeding
Application of a diagnostic likelihood tool such as the PSH-Assessment Measure
Review of medications and possible withdrawal states
redFlags: Sustained extreme hyperthermia or hypertension threatening secondary organ or brain injury
Features pointing to untreated sepsis, seizures, or raised intracranial pressure
Haemodynamic instability unresponsive to initial measures
reference.prognosis: The presence of paroxysmal sympathetic hyperactivity is associated with more severe brain injury, longer intensive care and hospital stays, and worse short-term outcomes; the paroxysms themselves usually diminish over weeks to months as the brain recovers, although some autonomic features may persist.
pitfalls: Anchoring on the diagnosis before excluding sepsis, seizures, and raised intracranial pressure
Provoking paroxysms through unrecognised triggering care activities
Undertreating hyperthermia and hypertension, allowing secondary injury
Abruptly stopping controlling medication and precipitating rebound storms
references: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: Reduce and cluster noxious stimulation such as suctioning, turning, and pain, since innocuous stimuli provoke paroxysms, and treat any underlying precipitant
Abort acute sympathetic surges with opioids such as morphine and short-acting benzodiazepines
Give scheduled preventive therapy with non-selective beta-blockers such as propranolol, central alpha-2 agonists such as clonidine or dexmedetomidine, and gabapentin
Add bromocriptine, or baclofen for associated dystonia and posturing, as adjuncts in refractory cases
Support with active temperature control, adequate hydration, and high-calorie nutrition to meet the increased metabolic demand
Monitor heart rate, blood pressure, and temperature to document and titrate against paroxysms, having first excluded sepsis, seizures, and raised intracranial pressure
Involve neuro-critical care and begin early neurorehabilitation, including physiotherapy to prevent contractures
